speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege in reference to the debate that took place in this chamber last Friday evening from eight to nine o'clock respecting the Bell Telephone bill, and the reports appearing in several newspapers. speakeroldname: Hon. COLIN GIBSON (Secretary of State) moved:
maintopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF ORGANIZATION AND ESTABLISHMENT OF PERMANENT POSITIONS

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF ORGANIZATION AND ESTABLISHMENT OF PERMANENT POSITIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words with respect to this resolution before it is adopted. First I want to make clear that I support the resolution and shall vote for it, and that also goes for the other two resolutions which I understand the Secretary of State will move today.
One little word of explanation on my own behalf, which I should like to give at this time, is this. There is in existence all the time what are known as the commissioners of internal economy. There is also in existence at the present time a temporary committee headed by Your Honour having to do with a revision of the rules of the house. Apparently there are some who have confused these two groups.
I am a member of Mr. Speaker's committee on the rules, and within the last few days I have actually been asked whether as a member of that committee I approved the contents of these documents that have been laid on the table. I think it should be made perfectly clear that the group referred to is the internal economy commission, which consists of Your Honour and four ministers of the crown.
With regard to the proposals contained in the document we are now being asked to approve, I am sure we all agree that what is in the document is good. Some of us, however, feel a sense of disappointment at some of the things that have not been included. I refer in particular to the repeated representations which have been made on the floor of the house for some kind of pension plan for sessional employees of the House of Commons. I have pointed up this problem by referring to House of Commons stenographers; but there are other sessional employees who should be similarly covered.
As hon. members know, every time we have raised this question-and it has been raised by all parties in the house-we have run into certain difficulties. When we address our representations to cabinet ministers we are told that this is a matter which comes under the control of the House of Commons itself, and therefore that we must deal with our own officers-in fact that we must make our representations to Your Honour. On the other hand we all know that since this does involve an expenditure of money, to which the government must agree-and that, I understand, is the reason for the internal economy commission-the officers of the house have to tell
House oj Commons-Staff

us that side of the story. The result is that we seem to make headway very slowly.
Last year the question of a pension plan for sessional employees of the house was discussed on the floor of the house a number of times, with the result that we were finally given the assurance that it would be given consideration. After the close of last year's session I wrote the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and placed in his hands a memorandum setting out one way in which this matter could be dealt with. That was not necessarily the only plan, but at least it was a concrete suggestion. The Prime Minister acknowledged receipt of my communication and assured me that consideration would be given the matter.
Several months went by without any announcement 'being made, so I wrote the Prime Minister on December 16 asking what had happened in connection with the matter. On December 23, 1947, he replied to me as follows:
Dear Mr. Knowles:
I have delayed acknowledging your letter of the 16th instant until there was an opportunity to discuss with the Minister of Finance the question of what further consideration has been given, during my absence from Canada, to the representations you made at the close of the last session of parliament with respect to the establishment of some kind of pension plan for House of Commons stenographers.
This is merely one aspect of the general question of the establishment of the House of Commons which is under active consideration at the present time. Mr. Abbott advises me that every effort is being made to see that consideration is sufficiently advanced to permit of decisions being reached and announced soon after the resumption of the session in January next.
Yours sincerely,
W. L. Mackenzie King.
A little while later, on February 14, 1948, having heard nothing further, I wrote again to the Prime Minister. The pertinent paragraph of my letter on that occasion is as follows: You suggested to me in your letter that any plan for pension arrangements for House of Commons stenographers would have to be part of the whole question of establishing of the House of Commons staff. I take it, therefore, that the announcement forecast in your letter would relate to the broader question, but I trust that it will include provision for a pension plan for House of Commons stenographers. May I inquire whether this announcement might be expected at an early date?
The Prime Minister did not reply to that letter in writing. But at his request one of his assistants telephoned me a few days later and told me on behalf of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance that my assumptions were substantially correct. The information I [Mr. Knowles.!
was given at that time was that two things were in prospect. One was an enlargement of the establishment so far as the House of Commons staff was concerned, and the other was the drafting of some kind of special plan for the sessional employees who are not covered under civil service permanency.
Subsequently-only a few days later; on February 23-1 asked a question of the Minister of Finance when the orders of the day were called. This is my question as recorded at page 1489 of Hansard:
I should like to ask either the Prime Minister or the Minister of Finance whether it is possible to indicate how soon we may expect an announcement about a pension plan for House of Commons stenographers.
To which the Minister of Finance replied: The officials of my department have been looking into the matter and have prepared certain recommendations which will be considered at an early day by the internal economy commission of the house, which has jurisdiction in these matters; and I should hope it would be possible to make an announcement very soon.
I held my peace for a considerable time, in fact until March 24 of this year, when an opportunity to discuss the matter arose in connection with estimates then before the house. Mr. Speaker was before the committee of supply, and I asked him specifically whether these matters were under consideration. His Honour said, as reported at page 2592 of Hansard of that date:
The positions of all employees of the house are being considered at the present time by the internal economy commission of the house.
.And later:
I have every reason to believe that all the employees will be perfectly satisfied.
I took it from what Your Honour said on that occasion, referring as you did to all employees, also from the correspondence I had with the Prime Minister and from the announcement made in the house on February 23 by the Minister of Finance, that we could expect at this time something along the line of a pension plan for sessional employees of the house.
I want to say I am disappointed, and I think hon. members generally will be disappointed, to find that what has been laid before us does not include anything for that purpose as was promised to us.
Since I have brought up the matter I believe I should say one further word. It should be clear that there are ways in which this could be done without putting sessional employees under the civil service. The House of Commons is jealous of the rights it exercises over its own employees; and we wish to retain

House oj Commons-&tafj
..nose rights. The employees themselves want it that way. I would point out however that it would be possible to follow one of two or three different courses. On the one hand a plan could be worked out by which sessional employees could start, from the beginning, to make payments into a pension fund, on the understanding that if they left in less than five years they would get those payments back, and nothing more, and on the further understanding that if they stayed longer than the period of five years they could begin to build up something in the nature of a pension.
Another plan would be to treat sessional employees, such as our stenographers, upon whom we depend so much, in the same manner in which we treat our Hansard reporters. The Hansard reporters are paid an annual salary. They are subject to duty in the House of Commons only during the time the house is sitting. They have permanency on that basis, and they also have freedom during the period when the house is in recess.
I suggest that would be a fairer and a better way to treat our House of Commons stenographers. Instead of paying them so much per day for the length of the session, as we do at the present time, I would like to see them paid an annual salary of, let us say, 81,800 a year. Give them permanency on that basis, and freedom between sessions, the same as wre do in respect of the Hansard reporters and certain other employees of the House of Commons. In this way they would have an opportunity to build up some protection for the years when they should be retiring.
As I have already said, we in the House of Commons are jealous of our rights to maintain jurisdiction over our own employees. We want the stenographers to be available when the house is sitting. We count on the fact that many of them will come back from year to year. I know that there are some who come only for a session or two, after which we do not see them any more, but I am more concerned about those who serve this House of Commons faithfully over a period of years.
It does seem to me that members generally should get behind a move of this kind. In anticipation of this matter coming up this afternoon I read again the debates which took place on March 28, July 7, and July 17, 1947. At that time we were pushed from one side to the other. We were told by the government that this matter was under the control of the house, and we were led to believe by the officers of the house that since it was a money matter, in the last resort we would have
to go to the government. In my view it is a matter for which the government will have to take responsibility. I do not see how Mr. Speaker can be asked to work out and be responsible for a pension plan. Obviously that is a matter for which responsibility should', be taken by the superannuation branch of the Department of Finance.
As I say, I do not like this idea of telling, us that these things are under our control when we know that the final control is in the-hands of those who have control of the money -I hope hon. members generally will support some pension proposal. I do not ask that the particular plans that I have offered be followed; I merely suggested them to indicate that something definite could be done and that we should urge the government to take action along these lines.
There are many phases of this whole question on which one could speak. There are many phases of it in which I am interested, but I shall not go further at this time. My reason for leaving it at that is the hope that by so doing we may make progress in connection with this one particular problem.

maintopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF ORGANIZATION AND ESTABLISHMENT OF PERMANENT POSITIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have not spoken before in this debate but speaking I believe on behalf of the Liberal party and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), whom I happen to have the honour of following, may I say that he is taking the right example in this connection. I understand that in August he is leaving for a younger man.
There are means available that would overcome these difficulties. I am not in the fortunate position that some are, but one who has. been closely associated with me made arrangements to overcome this difficulty in connection with stenographers and secretaries who have served us so well and faithfully. He has provided one with a pension for life. May I suggest to the Prime Minister that more young men be elected to parliament and then the secretaries will be looked after.

maintopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF ORGANIZATION AND ESTABLISHMENT OF PERMANENT POSITIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say only a few words with regard to this report. I agree that basically the report is satisfactory; it is a step in the right direction. But I do not think that enough hon. members of this house are familiar with the proposed establishment to criticize properly the plan which the internal economy commission of the house has submitted.
It is easy for us to pose as champions of the well-being of the employees of the house. I am one of those who perhaps has suffered
House of Commons-Staff

considerably through being around the House of Commons at all times. I have had to share with employees, who feel that they are aggrieved, their feeling of sadness because of their unfortunate position. However, as I look at the rest of the service outside of the House of Commons I must say-I think the employees of the house will agree with me-that conditions for employees in the House of Commons are not bad at all. Indeed 1 think this house gives employment which is remunerative. If the service of an employee is satisfactory he has a feeling of security which he would not have anywhere else.
Something has been said about pensions ' for stenographers. I am in favour of everyone having the benefits of a pension plan. However, I suggest to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) that he consider employees in the Department of Public Works and other departments who are employed at prevailing rates and who work the year round instead of four or five months and who do not have the benefit of any pension plan.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF ORGANIZATION AND ESTABLISHMENT OF PERMANENT POSITIONS
speechtext: Shame.

maintopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF ORGANIZATION AND ESTABLISHMENT OF PERMANENT POSITIONS
speechtext:
That is why I suggested at the beginning of the last session that a committee of this house should carefully study the conditions of work, pension plans, rates of pay and so on, not only of the civil service but of all employees hired by the crown. I agree that this plan is good because it is a step in the right direction.
I agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre in one regard. The members of this house should have something to say as to the establishment of positions, as to rates of pay, and as to any pension plan which may be adopted. I suggest again that at the next session a committee similar to the one which I proposed last year should be set up. In the meantime I intend to support the plan proposed by the Secretary of State.

maintopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF ORGANIZATION AND ESTABLISHMENT OF PERMANENT POSITIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when this report was tabled on April 29 I asked the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) if the veterans preference would apply when appointments were being made to complete the establishment. I should like to draw the attention of the Secretary of State (Mr. Gibson) to the fact that there are a number of veterans, both English-speaking and Frenchspeaking, who are employed on the staff during the session. These men may have been employed when war broke out, at which time they went overseas and thus lost their opportunity of being placed on the permanent staff of the House of Commons. I put in a special

plea for those men who served overseas and who have returned to the staff on a sessional basis. They should be given consideration and be permitted to compete for vacancies which are now being created, along with those who did not have an opportunity of serving in the armed forces during the war, who are not veterans but who had an opportunity of being employed on the permanent staff during the war.
I ask the Secretary of State that these veterans who are employed on a sessional basis be given opportunities equal to those given to the employees on the permanent staff.
Mr. JOHN R. MacNICOL (Davenport): Mr. Speaker, I rise to support largely what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has said, and also the additional remarks of the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes). I did not hear the proposal made by the minister, but I am sure it is a good one and is in the right direction. I do not know whether the stenographers who have been on the staff for some years are included in the list of those to be made permanent. If so, I am in accord with that.
I know there are a number of stenographers who have been here quite a few years. If they are not on the list, some provision should be made for them. It always struck me as being most unfair that these women who served us so faithfully in taking care of our mail should be turned out at the end of the session. Some consideration should be given to them. Whether they are to be put on a yearly rate or not is a matter for the government to decide, but I rose merely to say that I agree with the suggestions that have been made. I hope that in making the selection all employees will receive fair play, particularly those who have been here ten years or more. In my opinion they should receive more consideration than those who have been here only a year or two. I presume the minister will take that into consideration.

speechtext: We have not reached the increases yet. They are provided for in a separate motion.

maintopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF ORGANIZATION AND ESTABLISHMENT OF PERMANENT POSITIONS
speechtext:
The wording here is salary increases and establishment of the house. There is something radically wrong when even the minister does not seem to know what it is about. In view of the fact that none of us know anything at all about it, I think it should be laid aside for a little while until we get some information.
There is another question I should like to ask. How many years of service on the House of Commons staff have some of the stenographers who are now being made permanent? Why are the senior members of the stenographic staff not included in the list? I know of several stenographers who have had more than fifteen years of service on the staff but who are not included. There is discrimination somewhere. I think this matter should be left over until we get some information at least as to who these people are, why they are being appointed and a few other points of information that every member of the house has a right to have.

maintopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF ORGANIZATION AND ESTABLISHMENT OF PERMANENT POSITIONS
speechtext:
Undoubtedly, Mr. Speaker, the report that is before the house at the present time is sketchy. We cannot get away from that fact. It is also true that many of the members have been made aware of certain pay inconsistencies and various kinds of inequalities. It is appropriate that some more detailed investigation should be made of the whole matter of temporary employment by the House of Commons, as well as by the various departments of government throughout the country. While I agree with the hon. member for Ottawa East (Mr. Richard) that there should be a committee set
up to look into this matter, my opinion is that it should not be delayed until next year but should be undertaken at the earliest possible opportunity.
It comes to my mind in the discussion of temporary employees that at one time I personally took up in this house with the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) certain aspects of it.
I asked him why there should be so many employees in his department who were listed as temporaries, and how long it would be necessary for them to work as temporary civil servants before their appointments were made permanent. As I look at the estimates for 1948, I find a limited change in that regard. It would seem to me that five years on a staff as a temporary employee should be long enough to enable it to be decided whether the employee is or is not suitable to be taken on the permanent staff.
There is also the matter that was mentioned by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes). We have no assurance in this report, or no comment of any kind, as to what the position is with respect to the veterans preference for those who are on the House of Commons staff. Mention has also been made of the fact that there is no provision for pensions for members of the temporary staff, no matter how long they may be employed. There is also no indication of provision for automatic increases from year to year of service. As I look at this report, it appears to me that those at the top of the scale are fairly well looked after while those at the bottom are ignored.
I want to remind the house, with respect to the remuneration of temporary civil servants-and this is true right across Canada- that in some provinces temporary federal employees are paid salaries or wages which are below- the minimum wage of the province. That condition is backed by force of law, because provincial wage statutes-as for example, those in Saskatchewan-are not enforceable with respect either to employees of the dominion government or to persons who have contracts with the dominion government. A court decision was rendered recently in Saskatchewan to the effect that a temporary Christmas employee of a postmaster was not subject to the minimum wage laws of Saskatchewan, because the federal government was the employer. Those employees were getting less than the $18.50 a week minimum provided for by the statutes of my province. Such matters should be investigated by this committee.
Then with respect to employees of the House of Commons who are working part time only, provision should be made that after a few years they be put on an annual salary;
House oj Commons-Staff

and if it is necessary for them to travel to Ottawa from a distance, travelling allowances should be provided to and from Ottawa.
There is one final bone of contention, Mr. Speaker, that I should like to throw into the laps of the members of the House of Commons. In this building and elsewhere in the public service there are long-service employees who enlisted in His Majesty's forces. By regulation of the civil service commission, they were cut off from superannuation rights at that time, and on their re-employment those superannuation rights were and still are denied to them.

speechtext: I wish to say just a few words, Mr. Speaker, in connection with this motion. Mr. Speaker, I can only say in answer to the questions of my hon. friend that no employees of the House of Commons can be made permanent except by the house itself. The purpose of the motion before the house is to provide permanent positions for some 102 employees of the House of Commons which up to the present time have been filled by temporary employees. The establishment must be approved by the house itself. When the establishment has been approved the positions will be filled by the civil service commission; and, of course, in reply to the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes), I may add that in making these appointments the civil service commission will allow the veterans preference as provided by law.
This motion does not deal with the question of salaries. That matter comes up in a following motion on the recommendation of the civil service commission.
So far as this motion is concerned the establishment was approved by the commissioners of internal economy. It would provide permanent positions to a large number of temporary employees who have been employed for a considerable number of years as temporaries on the staff of the house.

speechtext:
We in this corner of the house have been silent on this matter, for the reason that we find ourselves in the same position as the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) and others-we do not know anything about it. I think I can say that that goes for almost everything that happens in respect to the staff and management of the House of Commons. I am not an old member of this house, but I am older than some, having been here since 1935, but I do not know the first thing about how the House of Commons in general is managed. I am going to have something more to say on that when the estimates of the House of Commons come before us.
I believe that the internal economy commission as now constituted is all wrong. I do not believe that the responsibilities devolving upon them should devolve upon Your Honour and four cabinet ministers. Each group in the house should have someone on that commission so that we could all become acquainted with what is going on. I do not know whether you know it, Mr. Speaker, but it would be a much healthier thing for you if all members could waylay a lot of rumours that go around concerning appointments for this and that, and a lot of other things that come to our ears about which we cannot do anything. We do not know anything, and we would not want to get involved in it anyway.
With respect to the appointment of, shall I say, the secretarial staff, I think, Mr. Speaker, that the present method of procedure is all wrong. Hon. members find themselves in this position, that their secretaries are appointed by somebody else. I should like to know who has 'the right to appoint anyone to work for me. I am the only one who should do that. The government assumes certain responsibilities that it has no right to assume. The government does not employ us. Extensive revisions are needed in the House of Commons Act, I am sure. The government does not employ us; we members of the House of Commons are not responsible to them. We sit here. They do not want us to sit here. We sit here because our people put us here and we are responsible to them. What happens with respect to the appointment of a member's stenographer? I am in a perfectly good position to discuss this, because I have no grievance with any stenographic help that I have ever had; it has always been satisfactory so far as I am concerned. If I had made the appointment I could not have done any better. But a principle is involved. Some Liberal member recommends a secretary whom I have to take.

speechtext:
On the orders of the day:
Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Secretary of State for External Affairs); I should like to take this opportunity to answer a question

asked on'April 29 last by the lion, member for Provencher (Mr. Jutras), as reported at page 3436 of Hansard. The question was:
Is the minister aware that the disastrous flood in Manitoba, particularly in the southern portion, has been caused to a very large degree, by foreign waters flowing north into the province. and that this disaster is a recurrent affair? Will the minister ascertain and tell the house whether the terms of reference which were issued to the international joint commission in January of this year, to investigate and report on the drainage basin of the Red river are broad enough to allow the commission to make a complete recommendation with a view to preventing the .recurrence of such floods?
Our information is that the present flood- or perhaps I may call it the recent flood-did come principally from international waterways whfth flow from the state of North Dakota into the province of Manitoba. While to some extent it is a recurrent flood, it had caused no disaster of this magnitude since 1916.
The reference to the international joint commission dated January 12, 1948, covering waters from the eastern boundary of the Milk river drainage basin up to and including the drainage basin of the Red river, does allow the commission to make recommendations with a view to preventing the recurrence of such floods.

If my memory is correct, there are two methods of dealing with land slides, one of which is to instal the block signals and the other to instal slide detector fences. I am informed that the Canadian National Railways propose to include the sum of a million dollars to instal a block system. I am not sure whether that is to be in the area where the accident referred to occurred, but it is certainly in the area in which these slides have taken place heretofore. It is also intended to instal slide detector fences, and they are proceeding toward that end immediately.

I should like to ask a
supplementary question. The purpose of my question this afternoon was to ask that the minister instruct-if I may use that word- the officials to proceed with the installation at an earlier date than that contemplated at present? The indications are that they will not be ready by next winter. I suggest that they be proceeded with at greater speed than is at present contemplated.

I am aware that, following the disaster to which my hon. friend refers, a report was sought. What the report contains 
I cannot say. I am informed however that following previous disasters which have taken place the Canadian National Railways came to the decision I mentioned a moment ago. It is the intention to proceed without delay.

speechtext: I should like to ask a question of the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply relating to veterans housing in Vancouver. Has the old Hotel Vancouver been discontinued as a hostel for ex-service personnel and their families? speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Reconstruction and Supply):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: HOTEL VANCOUVER-DISCONTINUANCE AS HOSTEL FOR EX-SERVICE PERSONNEL
speechtext:
As my hon. friend is aware, the old Hotel Vancouver has been under lease to the Vancouver rehabilitation council for the past two or three years. The rehabilitation council has operated the hotel as a hostel, and the government has given some financial assistance by way of meeting deficits. Last winter the council advised the government they did not wish to carry on the operation for a further time, and asked to be relieved of that responsibility. Early this year the property was sold by the Canadian Pacific Railway to another owner, and it was intimated then that the lease would not be renewed. The lease would normally expire on May 1 last. It was found, however, that proper arrangements for closing the hostel could not be completed on May 1, and a temporary lease for three months has been granted, to continue until July 1. The intake of tenants at the hostel was stopped on March 1 and the numbers in the hostel are shrinking. Eighty-five per cent of the married couples now in the hotel have indicated that they wish to take the alternative housing offered them by the government.
Married families with children have been given the first opportunity to take one of the six hundred houses now under construction by Wartime Housing in Vancouver. So far as single tenants are concerned, it will be necessary for them to find their own accommodation. That is also necessary for married couples without children. The numbers of tenants are normally shrinking down to a point where the residual problem on July 1 will not be serious, and I think no hardship will result.

Mr. Speaker, as we near the third anniversary of V-E day this debate on Canada's position with regard to external affairs becomes most valuable, perhaps more valuable than is realized at the present time. At the close of hostilities it was the hope of the world that
Supply-External Affairs

some intergovernmental organization might be brought into being which, by its collective action, would preserve the peace of the world. We, and I think all citizens of all democratic states, still clung to that hope, despite the failures of The Hague court and the league of nations.
Today with virtually a full scale war going on in Palestine we read headlines in the daily press like this: "Helpless united nations sees war in holy land". The situation, however, is not one where we should throw up our hands and abandon the united nations. The united nations today are possibly at a lower point in world opinion than at any time in their history. They are probably going through a lower ebb of public confidence than the league of nations ever went through until after the abrogation of the Locarno pact.
Despite the jibes, despite the failure, despite the veto clause, despite the everlasting talk, despite the obstructionism that has gone on in the united nations, the only hope for the security of Canada lies in some organization which will bring about collective security. That fact has been brought out through the passage of time. During the French revolution Talleyrand was quoted as saying: "In foreign affairs the best policy is to have no policy''. That supremely cynical statement would apply to what has virtually been the policy of Canada in external affairs until the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent) spoke the other day.
I propose to speak a little later on the subject of our trade relations with regard to external affairs, but I want to say now that we have entered into a new era in international affairs. It is obvious by what has happened to that part of the world under the domination of the Soviet empire. It is obvious that steps will have to be taken by the rest of the world to combat this definitely expansionist ideology if we wish to remain free.
One of the steps that are being taken is apparently the abandonment by the United States of the policy of no military alliances which has been in effect from the time of Washington up to the present day. It appears now as though there will be some sort of Atlantic union, or call it by whatever name you like, made up of the countries bordering the Atlantic ocean, whether they be on the European side down to Africa or on the American side from North America down to the outermost parts of South America. In that union the United States will play a dominant part and we, as her next-door neighbour, must be prepared for this new alignment in world affairs.

A military alliance which, as far as I can see, is inevitable under the present circumstances is something which the idealists in the first decade of the twentieth century and in the years after the first world war thought was an anachronism, an archaic revulsion, a return to the wars of the middle ages. I think we and the world have found that we have been driven by force of circumstances into some sort of military alliance with our friends. I see no other possibility at the present time than that this changed fact must be eventually realized.
I said that I proposed to talk about external affairs, particularly as they relate to foreign trade; because this, after all, is the point on which external affairs, relations between countries, first begin to disintegrate. The first troubles between nations are nearly always economic troubles. They lead to further friction and eventually to political action which, as has been said, is the mere forerunner of war. I shall therefore try to deal with the trade situation as it is developing under the present international relationship of the dollar economy and what, for want of another name, I shall call the barter economy.
After the first world war a European banker said to me that the breaking up of the Austro-Hungarian empire meant the end of European economy. He pointed out that the Danubian block formed a great central core of free trade upon which the economy of Europe depended. What he said has been proved to be true, because ever since the treaty of Versailles Europe has not known economic stability. Churchill, in almost the second paragraph of his "Memoirs", mentioned this. After this war there is a strong desire expressed in many parts of the world to break up the British empire, and in fact disintegration has been going on at an alarming rate. The British empire and the Austro-Hungarian empire had many points in common. They were both composed of many different races,- speaking many different, languages; and, as the Germanspeaking people in the Austro-Hungarian empire composed a minority, so do the Englishspeaking people in the British empire.
There is, however, one significant point which we must consider at the present time. The British empire has, despite the individual fiscal autonomy of the various component countries, formed a great worldwide core of trading nations. These individual self-governing nations have had their own tariff policies; but owing to the system of preferences they formed a world system of trade which, if it was not free, at least was infinitely freer than the trade of the rest of the world. If we

Supply-External Affairs
allow this group of nations to disintegrate, I fear that the same thing which happened to Europe after world war I will inevitably happen to the world after world war II. The parallel is significant. I mention this in the debate on external affairs, not for any reason of patriotism, but merely as a warning to show how dangerous this lust for ethnic selfdetermination can be to world trade.
During the period of the nineteenth century, which has been known as the period of the Pax Britannica, the 'beneficent influence cast by the reign of the pound sterling depended, in the final analysis, on British hegemony and an overwhelming preponderance of power ensuring some degree of peace; at least, it ensured, that wars would be localized. If, for want of other words, what I shall call the dollar standard is to play a similar role, it will be through the exercise of overwhelming American power on the side of justice. To some idealists this may be an unpalatable fact, but it is as inevitable as night and day, and we must be prepared to recognize it.
This brings me to a critical examination of the Marshall plan. Enormous publicity has been given to this throughout the world, and serious doubts have been expressed as to whether the United States was capable of providing so great a sum and so vast a quantity of material. Some critical examination of this point should be made. In any matter such as this, the salient point is the comparison between the expenditures and that of the total national income of the nation as a whole. This is called the gross national product. In 1948, which is the major year of the Marshall plan, the gross national product of the United States is estimated to be $230 billion and the total gross value of the United States gifts and loans is estimated at S9-7 billion, or 4-2 per cent of the gross national product. As a comparison, in 1919 United States gifts and loans, while only one-third as much as they are today, formed a greater percentage, namely, 4-5 per cent of the gross national product of the United States in that year.
These figures, which are the official United States government figures found through the Harriman and Herter committees, must for evaluation be compared with United States exports under normal trading. In the same year, 1948, United States exports of goods and services come to the sum of $19 billion, or 8-3 per cent of the gross national product. The significant feature is that the 1925 to 1929 average of United States exports of goods and services was $6-6 billion, or 7-1 per cent of the then gross national product. It is seen from this that even in 1948, the year of maximum
assistance under Marshall aid, actual United States exports of goods and services form nearly double the percentage of the gross national product. That is provided under the Marshall plan. The extremely significant point is that, even under the most unfavourable conditions, business between corporations and individuals is double that of business between governments.
The Canadian situation is even more intensified, because we are approximately three times as dependent upon foreign trade as is the United States. As a matter of fact our dependence is even greater than this, because, while our percentage trading position is three times as great as the United States, the loss of a third of our total trade would be infinitely more than three times as serious as the loss of ten per cent of the United States total.
This brings me to my next point with regard to trade, and world trade is the essential backbone of foreign relations. Our position in Canada is extremely hazardous because we are placed between the dollar economy of the United States and the barter economy of the rest of the world. Our shortage of United States dollars and the resultant austerity program, instigated by the present administration, is entirely due to our international position. I may say here that, while the austerity program has had some effect, neither it nor any similar program, no matter how drastic, can possibly solve the problem, because it does not tackle the situation at the root.
The drain on United States funds and continuing disequilibration of our over-all trade position are continuing and will continue, despite all the efforts the government may take along the lines of austerity and quantitative restrictions to trade. We are virtually sowing all the evils of state trading, and we have apparently learnt nothing from the past and are following the errors of the United States administration quite blindly.
I want to quote one paragraph of an article which appears in this week's Newsweek, and which I think is apt on this point. The article was written by Henry Hazlitt, who is a well known commentator and economic expert. It reads as follows:
It is disheartening that the President has learned nothing not only from our post-war experience in price fixing, but from the appalling consequences of existing price control in Europe. The most important thing America can do today is to continue to demonstrate to the world the enormous production possible through free prices and free enterprise. We must not cripple ourselves by imitating the very controls that have forced Europe to turn to us for help.
Supply-External Affairs

That is very similar to our position in Canada.
I want to mention briefly what is happening in Europe. The international trade organization which met in Geneva, was succeeded by the Havana conference, to be followed eventually by a further conference in Buenos Aires, drew up a charter for the rules on international trade. In order to make the I.T.O. and the Geneva and Havana trade pacts work, the barriers imposed by the complex mesh and network of bilateral trade pacts made by European nations must be overcome. The total possible number of such pacts, which are the very antithesis of the I.T.O. charter, by every combination and permutation between the nations of Europe is 231.
Since the war, no fewer than 113 such pacts have been made. Many of them involve countries with trade monopolies vested in government agencies, and many carried trade through the iron curtain. By this, Mr. Speaker, the European economy has virtually become a barter economy of bilateral pacts. These pacts are in fact an extended form of barter, but their very existence is a danger to Canada because they set up a pattern of trade which excludes any participation by Canada. Western Europe is working out a financial pool, a sort of international checking account to increase trade bilaterally amongst its members. The plan is conceived by the British who are the masters still of the methods of international banking.
What does this mean for Canada? It means that in Europe today there is a vast network of trading agreements between countries trading chiefly in commodities, trading between themselves bilaterally, at variance with all the pious hopes of the I.T.O., but also -and this is the important part-trading to the almost total exclusion of Canada, because the pacts are bilateral.
As I have pointed out, our per capita trade and our world trade done on a free basis constitute an imperative part of our economy; but, as we are suffering from lack of dollars, brought, about by our own stupidity, restricting our freedom of action, and as the rest of the world is rapidly forming bilateral barter agreements, despite the pious hopes of the I.T.O. and the Geneva and Havana conferences, our position is becoming rapidly more and more intolerable and our freedom of action is being taken from us.
It is at this point that I want to suggest one measure which, in my opinion, will restore our equilibrium of balance of payments in foreign

trade. That one move is the re-establishment of free markets, particularly a free currency market.
We have to restrict our purchases in the United States and more and pnore, through the clauses of the I.T.O., as well as through the artificial price structure set up by currency pegging in Europe, we find ourselves unable to buy from Europe, particularly from Great Britain, owing to the high cost of their goods. Incidentally, very recently the United Kingdom told our textile importers that it could not supply Canadian needs for textiles this year. It fell short for many reasons and by many millions of yards. This cost means little in a bilateral agreement which is really a form of barter. If you are exchanging one article for another it does not much matter how much you say your article is worth if you are not to be paid in cash. I should like to quote in this connection one paragraph from a recent article by Jacques Rueff, who was president of the inter-allied reparations agency in Brussels. This is the paragraph:
The disturbing effect of price control is nowhere more clearly shown than in the sphere of international exchange. The immobilization of the rates of exchange at a level below that which would be assured by the balance of the market dicourages export and often entirely closes foreign markets. For example, it is certain that so long as prices and rates of exchange remain fixed, countries which do not produce gasoline will not enjoy freedom of motor traffic. On the other hand, it provides maximum stimulus to the desire to purchase abroad. It therefore inevitably creates a hunger for foreign currency. Further, the position will continue to deteriorate so long as exchange rates are thus artificially determined. The deficit has a continual tendency to increase those prices which are free as well as black market prices, with the result that production is more and more diverted toward the free or black markets, thereby increasing scarcity on the official markets.
Our currency situation has shown a tendency to stabilize itself at approximately a ten per cent discount in terms of the New York exchange. This is encouraging, but there are discouraging sides to the picture. The investment of United States capital in Canada has greatly decreased in the last two years, and actually there has been a tendency, despite all restrictions imposed, for Canadian capital to leave Canada to seek investment in the United States. This is most dangerous. No one in his senses will invest capital in a country with a pegged or frozen currency. We see at the present time more and more pressure being built up against pegged currency. Mr. Aldridge of the Chase National bank, a close adviser of the United States

Supply-External Affairs
government, has stated that more realistic exchange rates must be brought about before the Marshall plan can be really effective. Mr. Harriman of the Union Pacific Railway Company, another close adviser, has said the same thing, and Mr. Hoffman, who I understand was president of Studebaker corporation and who is now in charge of ERP, which is administered by what is called the economic co-ordination administration, the ECA, has echoed these remarks.
There has been a persistent rumour that European currency revaluation was to be undertaken, starting with the Benelux union. Whether this is true or not, revaluation is inevitable. When this occurs our trading position will become more and more difficult. Mr. Speaker, before this happens, I believe that Canada should act.
What I am about to suggest may seem unorthodox to the present planners of our economy, but I believe it is the inevitable solution. I suggest two things. The first is that we free our currency from all controls whatsoever. This may seem a revolutionary suggestion, and there will be those who will say that by doing so we expose our economy to speculators in world currencies, and there are those who will say that our Canadian dollar would immediately sell at an enormous discount. Both these fears are, in my opinion. unfounded. In the first instance I believe it unfounded because the dollar has tended to stabilize itself at a discount of ten per cent on the free market in New York. There are those who say that this is a small market and that is not a true indicator of what would happen if we abandoned controls. I am informed that this is not so, and in fact the transactions on the free market in Canadian dollars in New York run to over 8100 million a 3'ear.
To say that a free market in Canadian currency would expose our currency to wide fluctuation by speculators is not, in my opinion, a possibility. We have one of the strongest international banking systems in the world, the personnel well versed in the business of foreign exchange. Furthermore, while our currency expansion has been considerable, it has certainly not been out of line with our productive capacity and our industrial potential. Thanks to the ability of our banking system, we have not inflated our currency. The soundness of the Canadian dollar is, in my opinion, appreciated throughout the world.
A third point is that we in Canada are producers of goods which the world must have. I refer particularly to the base metal group of
copper, lead, zinc and aluminum. We are also the foremost producer of wood products, particularly of paper. Add this to our agricultural products and we have a virtually impregnable position in world trade under a free market.
One other move which goes hand in hand with this free exchange is the establishment of a free market for gold bullion. This would mean that the Canadian dollar would be not only free but would be transferable into gold at the option of the holder at the day's buying rate for bullion, which would be determined by the law of supply and demand. With an option such as this, the Canadian dollar would then become the prime currency of the world, irrespective of the discount it would sell at in terms of United States currency. With the convertible factor, European nationals would do everything possible to sell in Canada; and I again emphasize the fact that private trading, despite all state controls, is still running several times that of state trading. Even individuals of countries behind the iron curtain are engaging in foreign trade.
To induce European nations to sell to us is the only way in which we can be paid for the goods we sell to them. So long as we engage in restrictive measures against traders, and restrictions in foreign exchange, we shall continually aggravate our dollar situation and at the same time make it more and more difficult for non-dollar countries to sell to us. With this in view and with our absolute dependence upon world trade, we face either freedom or bondage. It is my opinion that the move to free our currency should be taken at once. On this question depends our whole future as a free nation and to me it is the most important question in our entire external affairs position.
Stable exchanges are meaningful and useful only if foreign trade and investment are tolerably free. It is idle to say that, the pound is worth $4 if no one can use it. If nations continue to plan their internal economies they must plan their exports and imports. Free trade means much more than tariff reduction; it means a free internal market.
That, Mr. Speaker, is the position in which we find ourselves today. Our position with regard to the United States is well known. It has been discussed for many months in this house. Our position with regard to the rest of the world is just becoming apparent. One-half of the world is trading by barter; the other half is trading by hard currency. In Canada, fixed between those two types of trading, we shall find ourselves squeezed
Supply-External Affairs

almost to the extent of international insolvency because our trade will be so restricted. If we, by the method I have suggested and all the other methods, can possibly aid the freedom of trade, then our future and the hope of a continuing healthy economy on a rising scale will not be diminished.

Mr. Speaker, I consider it a pleasure to be able to participate in this foreign affairs debate, and I sincerely hope that I shall be able to' make my modest contribution to this debate on the relationship that Canada must bear and carry with other nations in order that it may exist, in order that it may survive, and in order that it may prosper. And we must not forget the necessity of maintaining peace in a civilized world. I hope Canada will pay a debt beyond a debt, in that it will help to suggest, promote and build international relations to a point where at all times we may be able to avoid war, the greatest scourge that can befall humanity when it reaches that point.
I want to take advantage of this opportunity to congratulate the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent) upon the lucid, definite and categorical expose he has given this house on the question of international affairs. I regret, however, that one of the principles the minister has accepted is that for regional defence we must work with and depend upon the United States, while on our large-scale policy we must also stand with Britain in determining our world position. I can understand the utility of this statement; I can understand its purpose; but if a nation cannot determine its own foreign policy, if of necessity it must fall between the conflicting interests of other nations, then it does not have the right of self-determination that it should have. Historically, actually and factually the right hon. gentleman could not help but accept the status quo with which we are confronted. By some twist of international mysticism, some ethereal conception of international life, the world has seen fit to divide itself into big fives, big fours, big threes and big twos, while nations which have contributed proportionately as much per capita, if not more, are ranked as secondary powers. Then perhaps there are also third-rate powers. In my opinion it was a grave international error to permit five powers, because of their size, to predetermine the life and future of the whole world.
I am a great supporter of the united nations, but I must say the veto was one of those traps none of the nations should have permitted to exist, even if there had been no abuse on the
[Mr. Adamson.)
part of Russia. No nation has ownership of another nation. No nation should be able to tell Canada whether or not she can decide, discuss or express an opinion on a certain matter, whether that is done by Mr. Vishinsky or Mr. Gromyko. No nation should pretend to have the right to say it will veto a certain question. It would be as though a criminal, brought before a court of justice, should tell the court, "I refuse to be tried, and I veto the question." That happened in Iran, in connection with Iranian oil. Russia invades a country, takes possession of territory which is not hers, exploits the people by a fake revolution; and when the question is brought before the united nations it is discussed always under the threat of the veto. Things like this make international fair play impossible.
I must also compliment the government on having established for Canada a muUt-partisan committee on international affairs. It is the logical thing to do. This parliament represents all of Canada. We have a common interest; that is, the preservation and wellbeing of Canada. It matters not on which side of the house we sit; our common interest is Canada. In arranging that all parties in this house be represented on that committee, directly or indirectly, the government has taken a unifying step; and I hope that in and for the future this shall remain a tradition with every Canadian parliament, that foreign policy at least shall be more than bi-partisan and shall be multi-partisan if there are more than two groups in the house. In this house we can act with unity of purpose, with strength and courage for the preservation of this country.
I wanted to refer to a remark made by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Cold-well), and I might add that I was quite inspired by his address. In his suggestions as to how to deal with foreign matters I found something rarely heard, that human value and those vita! principles common to all humanity, I found him logical, contrary to what someone else may say. I found his remarks pertinent; and when he said that he and his party had always urged that of necessity we must look to the winning of the peace, I was profoundly touched. It is true that the C.C.F. do not have a patent on that feeling, that they were not the only party to make the statement. It is true that it was common talk in the newspapers and on the streets, but the hon. member brought it to the floor of parliament; and I hope it registers with the policymakers as a basis for what shall constitute international obligations and international law.
Unfortunately-and I say this with all deference and respect because I know it is much easier to criticize than to put something into

Supply-External Affairs
effect-in my humble opinion no nation in the world had an international policy. It was a question of makeshift and mischief; "what can 1 get for my own country first, without any consideration of international justice?" For lilts reason we are in such a terrible dilemma today. The world is more confused than before the war with the nazis. The people do not know whence or whither, whether we are aoing or coming. They do not know what is the policy of one nation or the policy of another. The question is terribly complex. I agree with the hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson) that trade is one of the factors for international peace and also for war. It has been said that trade is the search for markets and that w-ar is the obtaining of those markets. But that alone is not the primary factor, and I do not think the hon. member made that claim.
There is a multiple, a complex system of international relationships as regards which, if v-e lose sight of one, we lose sight of all of them. It is for this reason that it is most difficult to establish an equitable system of international relations.
I have not seen nations stick together for ideological reasons. I have not seen nations stick together because they had prosperous trade. I have seen them break asunder on little points. For instance, at the time of the first world war Germany and England had a common interest in world trade. "Made in Germany", was beginning to get into the hair of Britain. When 1914 came something had to be done to lessen that trade. So that in this instance common interest is not a preservative of peace. Ideological or religious bases cannot alone keep it, either. The one and common ground must be the vital principle of the right of every -nation to exist. That must be the primary humanitarian reason. And if that is accepted, no nation can go wrong.
We feel now as we have never perhaps felt in the past, and we shall feel it keenly in the future. I do not say this because I want to praise anyone or for reasons of patriotism, but because I am thinking in terms of objective reality, when I say that at the turn of the twentieth century a void or vacuum was created in the world Britain ceased to be what she was in connection with foreign relations. Our objectives should be to help build the united nations into an effective international instrument for the maintenance of law and order and what I call fundamental human decency. Not only would such a policy redound to the credit of Canada as a nation, but since it offers the surest way to the establishment of world peace on the basis of justice and regard for human rights, it follows that it must be the wisest course for us to pursue.

Mr. Speaker, there are four main requisites of sound foreign policy for democratic nations: one, the guarding and preservation of the sovereignty of one's own country; two, the defence of the sovereignty of other nations and peoples who in the event of war would defend our sovereignty by defending their own; three, a proper and realistic defence policy; four, understanding among a group of nations or alliance of a number of powers strong enough to resist any coalition of hostile powers. Between world war I and world war II, Canada and the other democratic countries of the western world were guilty of inexcusable floundering with respect to each and every one of the four requisites of a sound democratic foreign policy.
Last Thursday afternoon, April 29, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent) made what I considered to be a speech of historic significance. In the first place, the minister's speech was perhaps the first creditable pronouncement of the government's foreign policy ever made in this chamber. Second, the minister's pronouncement is even more significant when we realize that it represents a complete reversal of the previous foreign policy of the government. Third, the government has fallen into line with the United States and the United Kingdom in abandoning the suicidal policy which brought western Europe to the brink of disaster.
If one had not followed closely the government's foreign policy in the past he would naturally be tempted to congratulate the government upon its present pronouncement. He said: "Ladies and gentlemen, the flaming sword of righteous Liberalism is about to descend on the decadent head of Toryism in the province of British Columbia." Hon. members will remember the posters which were posted throughout this country by the Liberal party and which promised a new social order. What did the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) have to say in connection with that new social order? He said:
In this new order, the rights of man will he determined, not by privilege derived from inheritance, position or possessions, but increasingly by men's own contribution through their own lives, to the common need and the common good.
The new social order. What is it? Increased profits, rising prices, lower taxes for big business and the Prince Edward Island trade union legislation. I am glad to see from press reports that that legislation is being rigorously opposed by the farmer organizations of Prince Edward Island and by the women's institutes. Taxation of co-operatives, no over-all security scheme; insufficient consideration for disabled pensioners and their dependents. Then it is illustrated in other little things such as the signing of trade agreements that take away the living of fruit growers in my own riding who have spent thirty to forty years in building up orchards without notice or consideration. That is what has happened because the policies of this country are carried out in relation to those of the United States. In the face of that record and that conception of a new social order, I am sure the people of Canada and a good many members of this House of Commons expect a more concrete definition of the government's new dynamic political gospel.

I see in yesterday's Montreal Standard these headlines;

The article reads in part:
Senator Joseph C. O'Mahoney today charged that pre-war cartels are being restored in Europe and that prominent "American cartelists'' are being given high jobs in the European recovery administration.

There is a great deal of serious consideration of the fact in Canada that we are to some extent becoming a satellite of the United States. They have a great part of our iron resources. I agree with that statement.

This is what we in this group have often referred to as world or international finance. It is a tyrannical force just as dangerous and as anti-social as communism.
Today we face a dynamic political communism and the menace of monopoly capitalism and international finance. My point of view and the point of view of many people in this country is that they present an equal hazard to the development of democratic freedom and economic justice.
Abraham Lincoln, with his remarkable foresight, sensed the beginnings of this money power. In a grave warning to the people of the United States he said he feared the financial power might grow and swell and pyramid until it and not the people owned the American earth and the American government.
In 1888 Grover Cleveland declared in a message to congress:
Corporations which should be carefully restrained, creatures of the law and servants of the people, are fast becoming the people's master.

The masters of the government of the United States are the combined capitalist manufacturers of the United States.
In 1938 President Roosevelt declared in a message to congress:
The liberty of a democracy is not safe if the people tolerate the growth of private power to a point where it becomes stronger than their democratic state itself.

I am criticizing that centralization of finance and monopoly capitalism which, in a crisis which threatens its existence will support fascism. There is some difference between the capitalist who invests his money in the country-who invests in an irrigation scheme, in the development of natural resources, hydro electric, public utilities and so on-and the one who invests his money outside it. He is a different type of man from the capitalist who is searching around- the world for foreign investments. The capitalist who invests his money in Canada is a different type of man from the one who invests his money, for instance, in a street railway in Madrid. The place of investment conditions their outlook. These people are internationalists just in the same sense that communism is international. Their loyalty is not to their country. Their loyalty is not to the nation of which they are citizens. You know the scriptural text to the effect that wherever your treasure is, there will your heart be also. These men who have investments around the world are internationalists. Because of those investments, their outlook is such that their first loyalty is not to the country in which they reside. That is why many of us consider that we must face this question which is confronting us squarely, the two perils -international communism on the one hand and international finance on the other.
I am not given to quoting at length, but there is a crisis within democracy, and I am sure that all of us, to whatever party we belong, are concerned about the preservation of it. Many of the statements made by the members I think show a lack of thought in this connection, and a lack of realization that we are living in a changing world, not only abroad but at home. I want to quote somewhat at length in order to put on record what I consider to be one of the most thoughtful considerations with regard to this threat which exists within democracy itself. This booklet I have in my hand is entitled "The Coracle". It is the official organ of the Iona community. The article to which I refer is written by Sir
George MacLeod, a personal friend of mine whom I have known for many years. This is what he has to say under the heading:
How to Preserve Democracy
I intend to read quickly because I should like to get this on the record for the information of the house. I continue:
How many ordinary folk grasp the real threat that faces "western democracy"-not from Russia but within its own consistency?
How many have faced the one condition on which it can continue to work? It is a byword that too many of our youth today are not concerned with politics. Modern youth are apt to say, "What is the use? We cannot affect the situation." Do we-or do they, for that matter -appreciate how right they may be, unless one condition is conceded?
Theoretically, western democracy is in the grayest danger of not being able to function. It is perhaps the strongest card in the communist's hand. Nor is it difficult to explain.
Parliamentary democracy, as we know it, only worked really well in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. The condition of its survival is a common agreement about economic principles, e.g., in the nineteenth century, when there was common agreement about the capitalist way of life, it was a workable arrangement that His Majesty's government should proceed in a conservative way and His Majesty's opposition should proceed in a radical way: or vice versa. "Five years in and five years out" meant that a healthy balance w'as kept between the more cautious over against the bolder road to progress: as parliamentary majorities changed hands. But the moment the issue ceases to be the pace at which we move and becomes a primary difference about the way of moving, our whole method is in danger. The movement, that is. when the difference between the two main parties is not political but economic: when what is at variance is the nature of the society we seek to build and not merely the expedient pace for building-parliamentary government is in jeopardy.
If ever a clearly capitalist party faces a clearly socialist party-then a general election every five years becomes a menace. For it is obvious that you cannot nationalize everything for five years and denationalize everything for the next five years, and so on, without resulting chaos. This is precisely what the communist and the fascist say: and men are foolish to disregard their thesis. It is because of this insight you get the extreme right and the extreme left pleading for "one party government". Take control, each says, and ensure that the other side never gets back. The opposition, in this view, ceases to be "His Majesty's opposition" and becomes His Majesty's enemy, fit for the shadows of prison rather than for a shadow cabinet. Only so, they say, can any country get on at all.
There is only one escape in our own country fro-m a similar decline in genuine party government. The one condition to assure a new lease of life for "government by alternating parties" is a mutual acceptance of a new economic basis. And it is the very nature of our contemporary world that demands w-hat we may call a socialized rather than an uncontrolled monopoly basis.

Once there is general agreement that the priorities of production are the concern of all and not a private playground then ve can afford a continuing argument about the pace of achievement. Those of "conservative" mind saying do not go too fast, those of a "radical" mind saying we must go faster: but both sides admitting the necessity, in our contemporary world, of an agreed over-riding thesis. Then in conclusion:
It is in this sense that it is a complete confusion to maintain that the issue is between "freedom" and "planning". Unless we generally accept "planning"-and confine the argument to the subsidiary issues of its pace-we will find ourselves bereft both of freedom of speech and freedom of association. Unless -we generally accept "planning"-and find a new area for the display of personal initiative-our parliamentary democracy will soon fail to function.
That does not necessarily mean a completely socialized state, Mr. Speaker, but it does mean that economic decisions concerning a large section cannot be left to a few men having greater power than the many. The enterprises of the state, whether publicly, cooperatively or privately owned, must be co-ordinated and operated to the public good.
I believe in the hope of world democracy. I believe that this hope can be realized for Canadians and for all people in our time, but I see this hope endangered by present trends. Many fear war; many expect depression; some await the destruction of the united nations. To those who admit the truth of all this and say, "This is a time for waiting," I reply, "We cannot wait." The welfare of Canadians and the welfare of the world demand that we act now.
Our industrial workers fear the insecurity of present employment; as their real wages fall with rising prices they suffer steadily declining standards of living. Our farmers fear that their period of prosperity is coming to an end. Our businessmen fear the instability of their markets. In the lifetime of my generation we have witnessed two world wars and two major depressions. But to accept the inevitability of war and depression is, to me, to deny democracy. The idea that personal or national insecurity is a necessary part of modern life, is to me, absolutely outrageous.

Since the end of the war, no debate has retained the attention of the Canadian citizens more than this one concerning our situation relating to external affairs. Any policy

elaborated on this matter will have far-reaching effects on the economic and physical health of our nation.
As a representative of a constituency composed of peaceful farmers and labourers deeply attached to their faith and their traditions, and as a member of the standing committee on external affairs, I feel duty bound to put on the record a few observations on that vital subject.
We are all aware that the present world is shared by two contradictory ideologies: firstly, the atheistic and totalitarian materialism, known as communism; secondly, the governments of the nations that believe in God and in the freedom of the individual, however they may be affected by a communistic infiltration, till now known as democracies.
It is quite abundantly proven today that the communist governments are dictatorships, in which the most oppressive powers are vested, and the leaders of which are tyrants who treat the individuals as the property of the state. Such a dictatorial system is in force, not only in Russia, but also in the surrounding countries which are now deprived of their most cherished liberties. It is well known, too, that an iron curtain is now separating the communist area from western Europe and the American continent. And this iron curtain has been placed there as a demarcation line, not by the consent or by the suggestion of any democratic nations, but entirely and exclusively by a totalitarian government, so generously assisted by western allied people during the war and without any due consideration for the welfare and the freedom of its subjects. This impassable barrier is erected by the communists so as to control every citizen behind it and to make them slaves of the state. Strategic posts are held by strong believers in the cause of universal communistic revolution. This barrier is disposed in such a way that it can be opened only on one side, and it is not on the side of the western bloc.
Communists only are permitted to come into our free world. The entry is forbidden to an international commission to go freely, visit these countries, inquire into their military forces and armaments and study the way of living of the different classes of their people. Such is the isolated oamp of the communist peoples. Even the ambassadors and charges d'affaires of democratic countries are held under polite supervision by the communist governments. What then is the use of having official representatives in such countries? I do
not see what benefit could result from maintaining costly representation near governments which offer no collaboration at all.
On the other hand, certain communist officials coming from abroad have fomented and encouraged communist propaganda and espionage in many American countries, and particularly in Canada. We desire peace and wish to avoid any cause of trouble and war. Since the ideals of the eastern and the western bloc are irreconcilable, why not adopt the policy of living peacefully at home, economically and politically? But this does not mean that we should isolate ourselves from the other democratic countries on this side of the iron curtain.
On the contrary, our external relations with the non-communist democracies should be developed and amplified as much as possible. For the time being, we have to give the fullest co-operation to these countries in order to stabilize their economy, as wTell as our own, and plan with them the best schemes by which to secure peace and prosperity in our western hemisphere.
Our free countries constitute a very large world and can live in freedom and prosperity by themselves. Let the communists try to achieve the same ideal in their so-called democratic closed countries. If we could be of any assistance to the people under the control of the Kremlin, perhaps we would be justified in trying to maintain our representation over there. But as long as it is impossible to collaborate and to have access to those suffering people, it seems to me that it is dangerous to expose our citizens to communist propaganda any longer, without having the least chance of demonstrating the principles of real democratic freedom among the people under the communist domination. The time has come, I hope, for all the non-communist countries efficiently to protect and safeguard their democratic and Christian philosophy.
Mr. Speaker, Canada has the right, and is obliged, to devote herself to the conservation of her political and national health as much as any individual is naturally inclined to safeguard his own life. What is the foundation of our national life? Our constitution, which guarantees to each government in this country, in its own respective jurisdiction, freedom of faith, language and speech, according to the rules established by the law of the land; freedom of union for workers; freedom of property and freedom for the people to elect representatives of their own choice. But this freedom must be exercised, having regard to the obligation of the citizen to respect the proper authorities, to respect the right of property, and the social order as it exists under our Christian democratic political system.
