Our national life is composed also of rights and obligations to which we are deeply attached and which we are duty bound to preserve.
Any individual knows that if he swallows poison he may die. Is it not crystal clear that if democratic nations are contaminated by the poison of communistic doctrine they will lose their freedom of creed, thought, and speech in a short period of years?
The enemy now menacing our democratic system is twofold: one, external, commonly called the Moscow bear; the other internal, which I may call a hypocritical and dangerous adder. The Moscow bear has shown its menacing attitude on many occasions in the last three years. It has done all it could to achieve its aim and ruin the free action of our nations.
Moreover, in international assemblies, the communist representatives endeavoured to introduce ideas which could facilitate their fight against us. The veto was resorted to whenever the democracies wished to have a right granted. No co-operation is possible between the advocates of liberty and those who try to destroy it. The Moscow bear is menacing, but the adder which creeps among us constitutes the immediate danger which we face!
This danger arises from many sources; first, the representatives who establish spying centres; second, communist groups in certain labour unions or other associations which are sometimes organized under so-called philanthropic, patriotic and charitable groups; third, the Labour-Progressive party, of which Tim Buck is the active leader; and lastly, all those who, intentionally or not, talk and act against the authority and the social order which we enjoy.
This is Canada's perilous position at this time; our country is menaced from outside and, soon, may be undermined from within. Having suffered two wars, it now deserves a fair, stable and durable peace. A conflict now would crush it between the two blocs of which it is the geographical link. Discovered by a Christian believer who placed her under the protection of the cross, Canada must pursue her course in order and in peace under the watchful eye of God. But to attain our goal, must we not disperse both the exterior and the interior threats? Why allow foreign powers, desirous of destroying our democratic system, to instal observation posts

in our country which might serve as a hotbed of intrigue and revolution?
When a neighbour refuses to receive us we do not invite him into our homes. Why maintain relations which might well be dangerous? Has the hour not come when we should each remain at home? Would it not be the best way to avoid war? When one is convinced of the bad feelings of an adversary it is better to avoid meeting him. It seems to me that if the communists guard their territory with guns the least we can do is to bar their entry, official or otherwise, into our country.
Once the doors of democratic countries have been closed to these official or non-official agents of communism, it will be easier to establish order at home. To do this we need the loyal and complete co-operation of all powers, federal, provincial and municipal, and of the truly democratic governments. Any government or party which uses communism as an electoral platform commits a criminal offence against the life of the nation. In sane co-operation we shall find the method of adopting social laws whose justice will heal the wounds which now afflict us.
It is not war, which will revive in the hearts of men the virtues of faith, hope and charity. It is not war, which in fact destroys more innocent people than criminals, that will eradicate from the hearts of men the roots of communistic hatred; and it is not on war, born of hatred, that charity thrives in this world. Only by keeping away the agents of communistic propaganda and establishing in our country a reign of social justice shall we consolidate a nation guided by charity, a nation from which hatred and communism will have been banished.
Should we, then, give a free hand to those within our country who endeavour to undermine our social order? Our criminal code provides severe sanctions for offences against property and morality. A robber is liable to imprisonment. All the more should people who attack not only our individual liberty but the basis of all our liberties not remain unpunished in the name of a false interpretation of freedom. Groups organized against the security of the state should be barred from society. Though it is impossible to read people's minds, we can judge them by their actions, their writings, their speeches; and we have sufficient evidence of these in communistic groups to prove their delinquency. It is the duty of every attorney general in every province of this country to prosecute them under the criminal code; and if the provisions of the code are not adequate, amend-

ments should be introduced to guarantee the safety of our nation. Moreover, even if it is not a radical means of suppressing communism, it is our duty to outlaw communistic organizations. Every communistic movement is clearly directed against the security of the state, and therefore is not entitled to be recognized as a political party. Otherwise we would be going against our natural instinct of preservation which is inherent to all societies and individuals.
In my humble opinion, it is by preventing every kind of communistic infiltration from the outside, by protecting ourselves against communism on the inside and by maintaining in Canada social order and justice that we shall contribute all the more to universal peace. In this way democracies will develop in an era of peace and order without having to resort to war, unless they are attacked. As for the totalitarian, atheistic system, it will crumble under its own weight, because it is based solely on hatred, injustice, theft and contempt for international and natural laws. The day will come when pressures are castigated and an era of freedom will be revived in the world. The doors of the communistic area will then be opened, and all the nations will live peacefully and good will shall cover the whole world.

Mr. Speaker, what I shall have to say on this occasion may sound a little idealistic and visionary after the more lusty speeches we have heard on this subject during the last few days. However I believe it is generally accepted that this debate has shown more ground of agreement on the part of those who have spoken than any previous debate on foreign policy, at least in my memory.
The chief subject on which I wish to speak this evening is what is known as the united nations educational, scientific and cultural organization. I want to refer to this for a few moments because of the uncertainty which seems to exist in the minds of the Canadian people, particularly those interested in promoting an organization of this kind, as to the intentions of the government in this regard. I would refer the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent) to certain questions and answers as they appear at page 850 of Hansard for February 4, 1948. The hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) had placed on the order paper some questions dealing with UNESCO. The first question was:
1.	Has the Canadian government made any progress since last session in. the matter of setting up a national commission of UNESCO?
Then other questions followed. The reply was:
1. No. It has been decided not to proceed at the present time with the establishment of a national commission for UNESCO.
If the right hon. gentleman has made any further announcement since that time, contrary to this reply, at the moment I am not aware of it, so I shall have to accept this statement as being the reply of the government. I believe it is not more than eighteen months ago that the same minister introduced in this house a resolution dealing with this organization, and at that time he asked hon. members to endorse Canada's membership in UNESCO. If there has been a major change of policy on the part of the government in relation to this organization, which to my mind is very important, then I believe this house should have the advantage of the inside story. We should know why there has been a major change of policy and what the intentions of the government are for the future.
To my mind this is a very important organization because, in spite of all the things we say about the balance of power, world politics, military alliances and so on, we always have to come back to the realization that thought precedes action. If it is the wish of the peoples of the world to have universal peace, then of course we shall not have to invest billions of dollars in armaments, national defence, military alliances and things of that sort. If it were possible to get behind the iron curtain which exists in the minds of the people on the question of war, and to appeal to their better nature-because they have it-then we might be able to bypass a great deal of the heart rending that has taken place in the last two years.
I wonder if the government has changed its policy in this regard on account of certain statements made by persons in this country who have attacked UNESCO and have, in effect, stated that it was a communist front and that the members of that organization existed in order to assist the imperialist plans of Russia, and things of that sort.
I hold in my hand a copy of a speech delivered on April 8 of this year at a Rotary club meeting in Hull by a gentleman named Ernest Dufour. He is here indicated to be chairman of the international service committee of the Rotary club of Hull. On that occasion he made this statement, a most disturbing one if it carries any weight with the government:
It was a sad day for me however, when as early as in 1946 only a few months after the birth of UNESCO I read1, firstly in the

newspapers and then in the Rotarian that Rotary international was entirely and completely behind UNESCO and were ^urging Rotary clubs everywhere to program UNESCO meetings to familiarize members with this important agency.
Then he went on to explain why it was a sad day for him when he found that Rotary international, of which, of course, he is a member, has taken it upon itself to familiarize its members and the public with the functions and objectives of the organization known as UNESCO.
Farther on in his speech he makes certain attacks upon the personnel of the executive of that body and, as a matter of fact, even attacks the secretary-general of the united nations, using this kind of language:
Lie has proved himself a reliable friend of the Stalin regime for nearly a quarter of a century.
In other words, part of his speech was to the effect that he deplored the activities of Rotary international in this country in the role it has been playing since the creation of UNESCO, in promoting its objectives and familiarizing its membership and the public with its objectives and with its program.
I am in no position to know whether the charges made by Mr. Dufour are based upon fact, or whether they are based upon his own personal opinion or perhaps his own personal prejudice. But I am sure the Secretary of State for External Affairs should at the earliest opportunity inform the house and nation as to how much truth, if any, there is in the charges made by this gentleman; and if the government has changed its position on the setting up of the Canadian commission for UNESCO, or if it has not changed its opinion, then of course the country should be made aware of it.
It is set out in article V of the UNESCO organization, under the title "composition"; that is, what it shall be composed of:
The conference shall consist of the representatives of the members of the organization. The government of each member state shall appoint not more than five representatives who shall be selected in agreement with the national co-operating body or bodies or national commission.	___
In other words, Canada's membership in the organization is based upon the setting up of what is termed a national commission of not more than five representatives. Naturally, since this organization deals chiefly with the dissemination of education in all its forms, the organizations in this country which have to do with education, such as the Canadian teachers' federation, the various teachers organizations in the provinces,

the Canada and Newfoundland educational association, and others, have shown extreme interest in this project and, as a matter of fact, have made representations to the minister to be represented on this commission.
Apparently, if the reply of the minister of Februarjr 4 is to be taken as final, the government has decided to drop the whole project and to do nothing more about it. If that is government policy, it appears to emphasize and to underscore the attacks made upon this organization by such gentlemen as Mr. Dufour, who makes an attempt-based upon what knowledge, I do not know-to throw suspicion and a certain amount of cynicism into the functions of this organization in order to turn the people of Canada against it.
Either there is something to the charge made by Mr. Dufour and others, or there is nothing to it. And I say the minister owes it to the house and the country to set the matter straight at the earliest possible opportunity, so that the co-operating body of educationists in this country, who have shown a great interest in this project and have shown their readiness to co-operate with the government, will know what the position is.
I believe it is only fair that some of the background of this organization should be given at this time, in order that we may judge for ourselves whether it is likely to be a subversive organization or one which may contribute something toward world peace and understanding.
Article I of the constitution of this organization is headed by the word "Purposes," and two chief purposes are set out, as follows:
1.	To develop and maintain mutual understanding and appreciation of the life and culture, the arts, the humanities and the sciences of the peoples of the world, as a basis for effective international organization and world peace.
2.	To co-operate in extending and in making available to all peoples for the service of common human needs the world's full body of knowledge and culture, and in assuring its contribution to the economic stability, political security, and general well-being of the peoples of the world.
If these two objectives were carried into effect; or, in other words, if this organization were successful in attaining these two objectives, then it would be doing something which at least ninety per cent of the members of the House of Commons have been trying to impress upon the government in the last few days.
It appears to me that the objectives of this organization are very worthy, and that if we are to play any part in co-operating with other nations in the organization, then it is about

time we made up our minds whether we are to be in it or out of it. Perhaps I should also say that UNESCO is not a new idea which arose after the close of the second world war, as seems to be the impression of some people who speak about it. As a matter of fact, as far back as the peace conference in 1919 one of the French statesmen, named Leon Bourgeois, brought up the idea of what he called intellectual co-operation, and suggested that an auxiliary organization be set up in order to bring together the intellectual co-operation of the various nations of the world.
Very little attention -was paid to his suggestion at the time. However, again in 1921 he brought the idea before the assembly of the league of nations at Geneva in September of that year, and was successful in having a resolution passed authorizing the council to set up a committee to deal with international questions regarding intellectual co-operation.
It might be valuable at this time to see what the objectives of this organization were to be, because they happen to be very much in line with those I have quoted from the constitution of UNESCO. These were later stated by the French delegation at San Francisco as follows:
1.	That peace among nations must be founded on comprehension and mutual understanding.
2.	That the united nations has a duty to see that cultures are made accessible to all men.
3.	That it is the duty of the united nations to facilitate the exchange and dissemination of knowledge about national, cultural and educational activities.
With a set-up of that sort, it would appear to me that this organization is a sincere attempt on the part of the membership of the united nations to exchange ideas on general education, science and culture among all the member nations. It does appear a little strange that anyone should consider it as being a subversive or communist front, particularly when we find that the Soviet union is about the only country not a member of UNESCO. I believe there is some confusion and the minister should set the matter straight.
What are some of the things that this organization could do? When I took part in the debate on the resolution when this was introduced in the house I stated that one of the things upon which Canada should insist in the united nations was the right of UNESCO or some similar organization to present a minimum program for peace in every nation of the world. There is much talk about the iron curtain, but sometimes I wonder whether we are taking full advantage of the facilities that we have to disseminate information across the borders of all countries in the world.
I believe that if the people of these nations were made aware of the full consequences and futility of war there are few dictators or tyrants who would set out to conquer the world. The people of the nations concerned would rise up in arms and would stop a war before it ever had a chance to start.
I have in my hand a sheet which was published, I believe, in 1945, toward the end of the war, entitled "World or War." This sets out certain information which I believe should be made available to every school child in every country of the world. This information would give the people some slight understanding of what is actually involved in war. We have the tendency, as soon as war is over, to talk about it as a matter of academic interest, but these are some figures of the casualties on the allied side alone up to May 31, 1945:

other nations. It would set out before them what they are facing. Of course the situation in another war might be more terrible than what we have passed through before.
There is, of course, the stumbling block which we come up against in every debate of this kind. People ask how we are to get that kind of information or that kind of program before the people of Soviet Russia. We are told that we are not permitted to go freely into that country and disseminate literature such as UNESCO could supply. When we come to that point there is almost a tendency to throw up our hands in despair and say, "There are two worlds; we are the one world and Soviet Russia is the other". It is considered that an impasse has been reached and that nothing can be done. Some of the speeches during this debate reflected such a tone of gloom that the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell) aptly called it a council of despair. I hope that this parliament can do something better than simply ration out despair to the Canadian people on this subject.
In my opinion there is a bright side to this question; there is a ray of hope. I think those who have studied the political history of Europe will agree with the statement which I am going to make but which may perhaps sound a little unusual or hard to believe. It is my view that there will be a political revolution in Soviet Russia in our lifetime. I say that, not because of any wishful thinking, but because I think it is in line with the development of that country and all other countries of a similar nature.
We accept Great Britain as being the cradle of democracy, as having long democratic traditions, and we are apt to forget that there was a time when they had to fight, not one political revolution but several. Perhaps the main difference between the development of Soviet Russia and Great Britain lies in the fact that Great Britain had a peaceful industrial revolution, sometimes called the bloodless revolution. Politically they developed through several stages of violence.
On the other hand, in my opinion the much talked of October revolution in Soviet Russia was not actually a political revolution. It had some political implications, but fundamentally it was an industrial revolution. It was the introduction into a backward and semi-feudal state of a new way of doing things. Because of the time at which it occurred, because of the terrific opposition to change, because of the war conditions in the country, it took on the character of a bloody revolution of carnage, looting and killing which went beyond

anything that we had seen so far in a revolution. I believe that the real political revolution in Soviet Russia is still to come.
When we speak of Russia or any other country we sometimes forget that we cannot throw all the people of a nation into one basket and say, "This is Russia" or "This is some other country." In my opinion there is a great difference of opinion among the people of all countries when you speak politically.
I refuse to accept the fact that when we speak of Russia we automatically speak of communism. There is a great difference between communism and Russia as a state. We must remember that there are millions of people-perhaps a large majority; it is hard to say how many-who are opposed to the system which they have or to a political system such as communism, who have democracy in their hearts and who wish to win freedom. In due time, with the right kind of encouragement and with the faith that the other nations of the world are with them and not against them, there will come a day when they will break the chains which hold them and will establish a democratic system in several stages in that country. It will not all be done at once.
Those who read history will remember that one of the early revolutions in Great Britain was that of a gentleman by the name of Wat Tyler. Of course there are many romantic stories told about the way in which Wat Tyler was killed and how King Richard offered to lead the revolution in his place. But behind the scenes the actual fact was that Tyler, as a type, was one of those whose idea of revolution was destruction, looting and killing. For several days the mob led by Tyler looted and pillaged in London. Then, of course, there came other types of revolutionists. We had men like Simon de Montfort. We had Hampden, Cromwell, Wilberforce, Wilkes and so on, each man in his way a revolutionist.
But as time went on, each one had a little more to contribute than he destroyed. I think if we draw a parallel of that kind with the Soviet union, we shall find that there are Ilampdens, Cromwells, Wilkes'es and de Mont-forts in Russia. At the present time we do not hear about them, but I believe that in due time their public opinion and various political mechanisms will slowly develop from a dictatorship, through representative government, and later on toward responsible government. I think we in what we call the western democracies should be doing everything possible to encourage those people rather than to throw them all into the same

basket as communists and say we will have nothing to do with Russia. If we take that attitude, then what we are doing is discouraging the very progressive and democratic forces which we should be encouraging, and throwing them into the same category as those who support dictatorship. By so doing, in the end we may be actually defeating our own purposes.
There is much that can be said about the possibilities. I have before me a book written by Professor D. Doroshenko, which is edited by Professor G. W. Simpson of the University of Saskatchewan, who also writes the introduction. Those who read this book, if they turn to chapter IV in which are discussed political conditions in the Kievan state, which goes back about nine hundred years, will find this significant sentence:
The political organization of the state was based on two principles:	the power of the
prince and the opinion of the population represented in the viche. a popular assembly akin to the Anglo-Saxon "Folk moot".
That is nine hundred years ago. Yet it is not greatly different from the type of development we saw in Great Britain, in which there was a sort of dual responsibility, the monarch representing the nation at all times regardless of who else is in power, and the popular assembly, or the people themselves expressing their opinions through a parliament of the people. Nine hundred years ago, in other words, the people of the Ukraine had already started on the rudiments of democracy. They have had, of course, an extremely rough time of it, having been invaded first from one section and then from another. They have lost their sovereignty several times and are now incorporated in greater Russia. I believe that is one part of the Soviet union where the real spirit of democracy has never died. Those people are still there. They are dreaming their dreams. They are waiting for the time when, with the proper encouragement and the sympathy of the western democracies, they will rise up again and will establish true democracy in that country.
I believe that if we can approach the problem from that angle it will bring the best results. I know it is not an easy angle from which to approach it; it is far easier to condemn a whole nation and say they are a bunch of communists or that they are a bunch of imperialists, that we must oppose them and see that they do not get anywhere. But I do not believe that is the kind of approach which will bring the best.'results. I think we shall have to try, if we cannot get through the iron curtain, at least to see through it, by what we can get from history and experience,
and encourage the democratic and freedom-loving forces, which I am certain are in that country in large numbers waiting for the opportunity to come upon common ground with the western democracies. Then it will be possible to have a real united nations, where there will be a real desire for co-operation and where there will be a chance for world peace. I believe that if that attitude were taken we might surprise ourselves as to how far we might go and how much we can accomplish.

It is not without apprehension, Mr. Speaker, that I take part in this important debate. However I will take the risk, if I may, of making a few observations.
First, I join with others, both within and outside parliament, in congratulating the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent) upon his detailed, most comprehensive and frank statement. It is indeed an historic pronouncement.
In directing Canada's affairs, this government and this parliament have the one objective in view: peace on earth for humanity. Ever since the end of hostilities, Canada has been alert in pursuing its course toward peace. Canada carried into the establishment of peace
Supply-External Affairs

and security the spirit of unselfishness and co-operation by which its magnificent war record was characterized.
It is well recognized that Canada discharges its obligations; and, because it does so, it is not seeking compliments. It merely hopes that other nations will follow its example and leadership and do likewise. Of course Canada aims at reaping some advantages in return: peace, security and freedom. Those who are most reluctant, or refuse, to see obligations where they lie-the more onerous the obligations, the more opposed they become-are often those who appear to long the most for the advantages. The paradox in this is that sections of the general public are often led astray as to where their true friends are. It is much easier, more popular perhaps, I admit, to join the camp of people who are always endeavouring to minimize obligations or even to by-pass them, although in their conscience they know they exist.
At this juncture, we are, I think, particularly privileged in having at the head of our Department of External Affairs a man who sets out the position with courage and blunt frankness. The people of Canada know now the exact score. In order to avoid what may become inevitable, that is another war, we must take certain steps which consist, in the main, in joining blocs of free nations, pooling our resources and providing assistance in material, money and men, if required.
As a matter of fact, no obligations emanating from our joining the free nations of the world in a self-defence scheme, under articles 51 and 52 of the charter, can be greater than those which come within the scope of chapter VII, article 42 and others of the united nations charter, which was approved unanimously by this parliament after a full debate in October,
1945.
On March 17, 1948, a fifty-year treaty of economic and social collaboration and collective military aid, was signed in Brussels, by Britain, France, Belgium, Holland and Luxembourg. It is a collective security treaty against aggression. The short speeches that were made after the signing of the treaty by the representatives of the countries concerned indicate the compelling motives behind it. Mr. Spaak of Belgium said:
We do not intend to interfere in the internal affairs of anyone, but demand of all others the same abstention. . . By pooling our resources and our potential, we shall be the equals of the greatest powers in the world.
Among other things, Mr. Bidault of France declared:
On the road from Paris to Brussels, there is hardly a town or village whose name is not

also that of a battle. This tragedy has lasted long enough. We are here to put an end to it, with all the means in our power-means which we will employ to the limit-to come to each other's aid.
At Bogota, in the afternoon of Friday, April 30, twenty-one nations signed a pact which enlists them also as a unit of resistance against communist expansion. These twenty-one nations of the western hemisphere have adopted conventions and agreements, the whole of which may be regarded as a regional arrangement under articles 51 and 52 of the united nations charter. It is reasonable to assume that the nations of the middle east may eventually bring their league to the standard of a regional arrangement within the ambit of articles 51 and 52 of the charter.
The free world is purchasing a carefully prefabricated house, the parts of which will eventually and shortly be assembled. To the western union, the British commonwealth of nations, the Pan-American union, the Arab league, add up the few remaining free nations, and you obtain a federation of regional blocs including all the member-states of the united nations, except the U.S.S.R. and her satellites.
If such is the contemplated objective-and no doubt it is-it will be indeed a delicate operation to perform. In the next few months the free nations of the world, organizing themselves in order to assure their survival, will be skating on thin ice. It will be all the more dangerous, because they will have to act speedily.
I do not think, sir, that anyone can state that there will be no war in the near future. If it is so, it is only fair that the people be told. The U.S.S.R. may not want war; it may not be ready for a war. Perhaps they want war, and perhaps, compared with the strength of the opposing camp they are ready for a war.
Of course we cannot assess the possibilities of a war in present times as we did in the past. Hitler had over-run several countries with the aid of his fifth columns before the allies united and even fired a single shot. At the end of the hostilities we entered a race with the other allied countries for the demobilization of our forces and we won. The government was criticized for not having carried it out faster. While the demobilization race was on, we could read in our papers that parachute jumping contests were being held in the U.S.S.R. We hardly heard about any large-scale demobilization being carried on there.
We turned to the united nations for peace and security. After three years of effort, we find ourselves in a position as precarious as that which prevailed in 1939. The U.S.S.R

Supply-External Affairs
has adopted Hitler's tactics and gradually extends its domination over new territories. If permitted to carry on indefinitely this sneaky process of aggression, of course the U.S.S.R. will go on exclaiming that it does not want war, because in such circumstances it does not need war. It is up to us either to decide that we call Mr. Stalin and tell him that we bow to his ruling, in which case we would not have to debate commitments, et cetera-he would take care of all that for us-or to decide to unite with others against communist expansion, and along with them to undertake necessary obligations, the amplitude of which can be determined only by the needs of the hour. These needs will be assessed and listed by men, leaders in their country as in our own, who took part in the demobilization race to which I referred a moment ago, men who are not militarists, or aggressors, men who want freedom as we know it and cherish it, for their fellow countrymen and for themselves.
In trying to check the plan of aggression pursued by the U.S.S.R., we may be compelled to resort to military action. We cannot put aside that possibility. We must bear in mind the purport of the extraordinary measures adopted by the United States government in the last few' months. Pending the enactment of universal military training, the United States has re-enacted temporarily selective service legislation affecting approximately three million young men between twenty and twenty-six years of age. My understanding is that a line has been drawn and that the Moscow planners must take notice that they can go no farther.
The temporary setbacks suffered by communism in France and Italy have given us some ground for rejoicing. I venture to say that if communists had won the last general elections in Italy, the United States marines holidaying in the Mediterranean might have ceased to be tourists. A communist victory in Italy might have been counteracted by action which would have been tantamount to a declaration of war. Communist victories in any country that is now free must not take place. The free nations program must go farther if it is to observe the high objectives and principles of the united nations charter; it must contemplate the liberation of the people now under communist rule. It must aim at wiping out communism from this earth, so that once it is dislodged from its present headquarters, the Kremlin, it is not allowed to spring and flourish from elsewhere.
I have the opportunity, like many hon. members, of meeting people who take an active part in international affairs study groups. In
the months preceding the last session of the united nations assembly, some of them often felt that the U.S.S.R. was misunderstood, that the Russian diplomats were suspicious of the western powers, because they had an inferiority complex or for some other reason. They always had an excuse or a justification for a U.S.S.R. move, which by others were considered as further indications that the U.S.S.R. simply did not v'ant to co-operate unless they had their own way.
These people were not communists, or Russian sympathizers any more than Mexican sympathizers. They were Canadians trying to judge international events without prejudice and partiality. Their lack of information or their anxiety for peace and security probably impaired their judgment.
Only a few days after the opening of the last session of the general assembly, at Flushing Meadows, New York, at which I had the privilege to attend, I heard several delegates voice the opinion that the united nations could not make any progress because of Soviet obstruction tactics, and that they should make up their mind to carry on without them.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs translated, in his address before the assembly, the anxiety of a majority of delegations by sounding a warning note. He said:
Nations, in their search for peace and1 cooperation, will not and cannot accept indefinitely and unaltered a security council which was set up to ensure their security, and which, so many feel, has become frozen in futility, and divided by dissension. If forced, they may seek greater safety in an association of more democratic and peace-loving states, willing to accept more specific international obligations in return for greater national security. Such associations, if consistent with the principles and purposes of the charter, can be formed within the united nations. It is to be hoped that such a development will not be necessary. If it is unnecessary, it will be undesirable. If. however, it is made necessary, it will take place. Let us not forget that the provisions of the charter are a floor under, rather than a ceiling over, the responsibilities of member states. If some prefer to go even below that floor, others need not be prevented from moving upwards.
Very patiently and with dignity, delegates laboured at achieving some constructive solutions of world problems, but Soviet obstruction tactics persisted and frustrated their efforts.
The debates which took place, both in the general assembly and in the committees, revealed the insurmountable difficulties of trying to get along with people who simply do not want to co-operate.
Today we all realize that it is not unfair to lay the blame on the Soviet group. That is where it belongs.
Supply-External Affairs

There is, in the house and outside, at public meetings, during electoral campaigns, a practice which consists of calling the other fellow a communist. This sort of tactic achieves nothing but the creation of confusion in the public mind as to who is really a communist. In the accusations that have been made from time to time, no single member of the house has been spared; everyone is a communist. There was once a shepherd who, for his own amusement, decided to yell, "Wolves! Wolves!" To his assistance came promptly all the neighbouring shepherds. There were no wolves. He called again. They came and there were no wolves. He called a third time. There were wolves but the shepherds did not come. We might, with advantage, remember the lesson taught by the fabulist.
The minister has already explained the difficulties of Canada in its attitudes and their interpretation by other powers as being a satellite-like attitudes of the United States or the United Kingdom. If because of our common background, culture, traditions, institutions and interests, we happen to think often alike, our own people should not conclude that, we cannot stand up on our own. In a Montreal paper, a parliamentary correspondent wrote last week that Canada was moving from the orbit of Great Britain to enter the orbit of the United States. Canada is a member of the international community, move it from one orbit to the other if you wish. As the minister said on Thursday last, "This country is now inevitably and inextricably involved in the full current of international events." Those who might argue neutrality or nonparticipation in this worldwide crusade against communism will do so in the hope perhaps of obtaining some political advantages or in order to save their faces because they opposed war expenditures and participation too recently, or because they may find it healthy-to prevent abuses, they will say-to promote as a check encouragement to resistance to commitments of any kind. Before they embark, however, on a campaign of any sort, I wish they will pause to digest thoroughly the statement made by the minister last Thursday and await other developments which will further clarify the situation.
I address the same request to those who might be tempted to advocate greater commitments than necessary, or to exaggerate the danger. The press especially will, I am sure, in the circumstances exercise its freedom with a proper sense of responsibility and accountability to the people.
A majority in this country, in every section of this country, realizes, I believe, that isolation is impossible and that these are times without parallel in the history of mankind.

It is particularly significant and gratifying that the youth of this country should be so keen on studying international developments. Last March, at the invitation of the University of Montreal students, delegates representing student bodies from fifteen Canadian universities organized a federation of the international relations clubs of our Canadian universities. I am convinced that these young men and women, whom I had the pleasure of meeting, will play a leading part, in their respective communities, in the days ahead. Such is the case also for the junior boards of trade and chambres de commerce des jeunes all across the country. A delegation of this progressive youth movement has just returned to Canada after having participated, with great ability and honour, in the international congress of junior chambers of commerce, held at Rio de Janeiro. They, too, will be in the vanguard of the crusade which is now getting under way.
But in order to play their full part, they must be fully informed. I suggest that the widest distribution possible be made of the historic statement delivered last Thursday by the minister. Service clubs, business clubs, women's associations, labour groups, farmers' unions, branches of the Canadian Legion, youth organizations and others should be provided with copies of that statement for their membership. The press and radio should report it verbatim. The united nations association is, I think, the one association which could most effectively do a job of informing the public. They are engaged in this very wmrk, and the officers of the association would, I am sure, be only too glad to help more than they are able to do at present. The united nations association, in Canada, with very little money has done magnificent work. I trust that the government will give to that association this year greater recognition and support.
